elements.text: Captain's failure to reject takeoff in a timely manner due to excessive nosewheel steering tiller inputs causing loss of directional control
Inadequate Boeing 747 slippery runway operating procedures developed by Tower Air and Boeing
Inadequate fidelity of B-747 flight training simulators for slippery runway operations
Captain's reapplication of forward thrust before departing the runway, contributing to severity
Flightcrew properly certificated and qualified
Air traffic control personnel properly certificated and qualified
Airplane properly certificated, equipped, and maintained (except FDR system)
Captain's decision to attempt takeoff on runway 4L was appropriate
Asymmetric thrust was not a factor
Captain's overcontrolling of nosewheel steering through the tiller caused deviation from centerline
Captain relied on right tiller inputs then applied insufficient/untimely right rudder inputs
Current Boeing 747 operating procedures provide inadequate guidance regarding loss of directional control at low speeds on slippery runways with tiller use
Tower Air procedural change to eliminate guarding tiller during takeoff roll reduces overcontrol likelihood
Current Boeing 747 flight manual guidance is inadequate about when to reject takeoff after lack of directional control response
Improvements in slippery runway handling fidelity of flight simulators are needed and feasible
Captain's failure to reject takeoff in a timely manner was causal to the accident
Inadequate Boeing 747 slippery runway operating procedures and simulator fidelity contributed to the cause
Captain abandoned reject attempt by restoring forward thrust, contributing to severity
Material or installation of secondary latches in galleys was inadequate
Ambiguity in situation led to fewer brace commands than possible
Tower Air flight attendant procedures provided inadequate guidance on communication during impact
Tower Air flight attendant galley security training was inadequate due to lack of hands-on training
Tower Air did not perform FDR functional test, resulting in loss of critical data
Tower Air maintenance program deviated from established procedures
Tower Air airworthiness surveillance and reliability programs were performing inadequately
Tower Air operated with inadequate management structure
FAA inspectors were overburdened and surveillance program was inadequate
ATC failure to provide friction data did not contribute to the accident
Issue of correlating stopping performance with friction measurements should be revisited
